intro: Hi, I'm Maya, and this is the AI News Brief for Friday, October ninth, twenty twenty-six.
And I'm Leo. Today, Google wants Gemini to be a coworker with its own email address, Anthropic launches a cyber defense mission, and StepFun's huge new model lands on OpenRouter.
We also have an update on OpenAI's math release, a one point eight billion dollar bet on biology data, and an unpatched security hole that inference teams should check today.
stepfun-step-5: First up, model updates. The Chinese lab StepFun now has Step five Preview available on OpenRouter, and it was on the Hacker News front page this morning.

The headline number is six hundred billion parameters, but only twenty-seven billion are active for each token. That's a mixture of experts design. The model is split into many specialist sub-networks, and a router picks a few of them for each token. So you get the knowledge of a very large model, with the running cost closer to a mid-sized one.

It has a one million token context window. Pricing on OpenRouter is one dollar per million input tokens and two dollars and seventy cents per million output tokens, and cached input is five cents per million.

The caveat is the open weights. StepFun's roadmap says weights arrive on October fifteenth, but the Hugging Face repository is still empty and no license has been published. On Artificial Analysis it scores forty-four on the Intelligence Index, so treat it as a strong, cheap option to test, not a frontier replacement.
liquid-d1: Next, Liquid AI released two open-weight models called d one. There's d one three B, which takes text and images, and an experimental d one omni at six hundred million parameters, which can also take audio.

These are decision models, a category we've been tracking all month. Instead of writing an answer word by word, the model reads the input once and directly returns a structured choice, like yes or no, a label, or a score. One forward pass, no text generation.

That makes them fast. Liquid reports about sixteen milliseconds per question on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, and about fifty milliseconds on the small Jetson Orin Nano. Those are vendor numbers. An independent run on four hundred cases measured about seventy-four percent accuracy.
Check the license before you ship. The model cards list Liquid's LFM one point zero license, not Apache. But if you're doing routing, moderation or sensor checks on a device, this is worth a look.
gemini-free-flash-lite: One more model change, and it starts today. Free users of the Gemini app, on personal accounts, now only get Flash-Lite, the smallest of Google's three models. Flash and Pro are gone from the free picker.
The four dollar and ninety-nine cent AI Plus plan also loses Pro, but on a later date that Google will email to subscribers. The nineteen ninety-nine AI Pro plan keeps all three models.

Google is also adding low, medium and high effort settings to every model. Higher effort gives more thorough answers but uses up more of your compute-based limit, which resets every five hours up to a weekly cap.
For developers, the reports we saw don't mention any change to the Gemini API. But if your team leans on free consumer Gemini for quick work, expect a quality drop starting today.
openai-math-withdrawals: On to research. First, an update on OpenAI's big math release. Earlier this week OpenAI posted seven hundred and twenty-two manuscripts written by an unreleased internal model, and mathematicians pushed back.

Now three of them have been withdrawn. A sign error, literally a plus that should have been a minus, broke a key cancellation step in a paper on Weil classes on abelian eightfolds. Two other papers, on K three surfaces, built on that construction, so they were pulled too.

The catalogue now lists seven hundred and nineteen manuscripts in three hundred and seventy-two families. Fourteen more were revised to repair proofs or correct statements. The withdrawn versions stay online with notices explaining the gaps.

The lesson is about dependency chains. One bad step in a foundational result can quietly break everything built on it. AI can produce math at scale, but checking it still needs audit trails and real verification.
virtual-biology-initiative: Next, a big data bet for biology. Biohub, the U.S. Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health and several tech partners expanded the Virtual Biology Initiative, with one point eight billion dollars in commitments.

Here's the breakdown. Biohub puts in five hundred million. The Department of Energy commits more than five hundred million over five years. NIH coordinates more than five hundred million, but that's existing funding and datasets, not new money. And Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta add three hundred million combined.
The goal is open, standardized data on how cells respond when you intervene, for example with a drug or a genetic change, across many more cell types than anyone has measured.

Why it matters: predictive biology models are limited by data, not model size. A shared, AI-ready resource with common standards could do for cell biology what large public datasets did for protein structure.
long-wam: The top paper on Hugging Face today is from NVIDIA. It's called Long-WAM, and it's about world-action models for robots.

A world-action model predicts what the world will look like next and what action to take, together. The question here is how much past video a robot should remember. More history helps it understand motion and task progress, but it can slow down each decision.

They first pretrained a video model on robot and first-person videos without any action labels, then adapted it to output actions. On the RoboCasa benchmark, going from no history to nineteen point two seconds of context raised success from sixty-three point three percent to seventy-eight point seven percent.

And it stays fast. Each action step takes about one hundred and seven milliseconds on an RTX fifty ninety. On real robots it hit ninety-five percent on a dynamic cup stacking task, where two baselines failed all twenty tries. These are the authors' numbers, so watch for independent replications.
remory: Last research item, and it's very practical for agent builders. It's called REMORY.
Long-running agents eventually fill their context window, so they compact it. They replace the history with a text summary. The problem is that a summary drops details the agent needs later.

REMORY adds a small neural network that writes a handful of learned memory tokens after the summary. These aren't words. They're vectors that help a frozen language model behave almost as if it still had the full history. On one benchmark it came close to full-context performance while using only five point two percent of the input positions.

With Qwen three point eight twenty-seven B and GLM five point three Flash, it cut repeated tool calls and tool errors on BrowseComp and Terminal-Bench. The code and adapters are public, so it's something you can actually try.
gemini-universal-agent: Now business applications, and the biggest story of the day. At its Gemini at Work event, Google announced a universal Gemini agent, starting with businesses.

The idea is that you give it objectives, not step by step instructions. It plans the work, uses skills and tools, and delegates pieces to subagents. A tasks inbox shows its reasoning, the code it ran, and its progress.

The part people are talking about is identity. An agent can get its own Workspace account, with an email address, calendar and Drive. You can tag it, email it, or add it to a group chat, and its actions show up in audit logs under its own name, not a person's.

It picks a model for each task, and you can also choose Anthropic's Claude. There are real-time spend caps and project budgets that pause an agent when money runs out. The caveats are no pricing, no general availability date, and consumers come later.
anthropic-cyber-mission: Anthropic launched what it calls the Cyber Mission, a long-term effort to help defenders. It builds on the Cyber Verification Program we covered earlier this week, and starts with two areas.

First, critical infrastructure. A new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program brings Claude models, on-site engineers and threat research to security providers for things like power grids and water systems. There are eleven founding partners, including CrowdStrike, Dragos, Palo Alto Networks, Deloitte and Rockwell Automation.

Second, open source. OSS Scanner is a free, opt-in service, inspired by Google's OSS-Fuzz. Enrolled projects get periodic scans, and each report has a proof of concept, an explanation and a suggested fix.

Anthropic expects a true positive rate above ninety percent, but the reports go out without human review, so severity ratings can be wrong. It's meant for projects that can handle the volume. Anthropic also says plainly that operational systems often can't be patched quickly.
nous-hermes-series-b: Last business story. Nous Research raised a ninety million dollar Series B at a one point five billion dollar valuation, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Nous makes Hermes, an open-source agent under the MIT license. It's not a single model, it's an agent you can point at different models. It's hugely popular with developers, with over two hundred thousand GitHub stars as of July.

The money goes toward a business offering. It adds team controls, shared skills, model choice, single sign-on, service level agreements, and private or on-premises deployment, so company data stays on your own infrastructure. Investors include NVIDIA and Microsoft's M twelve.
Enterprise pricing isn't public. But for teams that want an agent they can self-host and inspect, it's now a more serious option next to the hosted agents from the big labs.
deepseek-v4-1-flash: Now, popular models right now. First, an update on DeepSeek V four point one Flash. It's the number one story on Hacker News today, with more than eight hundred points.

The post is a developer's report after a month of heavy use across a dozen projects. The claim is that for day to day work it's nearly indistinguishable from Claude Opus, and that the industry is ignoring it because it equates price with quality.

The cost gap is the point. The author estimates a routine file organization task at about three tenths of a cent, versus about one dollar on a frontier model. They still use Opus five point five now and then for a final code review.
Keep in mind this is one person's experience, not a benchmark. But it's a good prompt to rerun your own evals on cheaper models. You can use it through DeepSeek's API, and the weights are open.
whistle: Next is Whistle, from Cactus, with about eight hundred points on Hacker News. It's a speech to text model that fits in sixteen point nine megabytes.

For comparison, Whisper base is about one hundred and forty-five megabytes, so Whistle is roughly a ninth the size. It handles seven languages, English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch and Polish, and it gives word level timestamps.

It runs on a CPU. On an Apple M four Pro, the first token comes in about eleven milliseconds. Cactus says it beats Whisper base on several benchmarks, but Whisper base still wins on others, like TED talks and meeting audio.
It's Apache two point zero, and there are prebuilt engines for seventeen platforms, including phones and the browser. If you need offline transcription on small devices, it's a cheap thing to try.
ltx-2-5: The last popular model is LTX two point five from Lightricks. It's in the Hugging Face top ten, with about one point seven million downloads.

It's an open video model of roughly twenty-two billion parameters, based on its file names. It generates video with synchronized audio from text, images or video, and it can do multiple shots while keeping the characters, lighting, voice and style consistent across cuts.
Output is around ten eighty p, and you can go to four K with an upscaler. It runs in Python, ComfyUI or Diffusers, and there's a hosted API too.
Watch the license. It's free for commercial use if your company makes under ten million dollars a year. Above that, you need a paid agreement.
lmcache-cve: Finally, implementing AI, and we start with a security warning. JFrog disclosed a critical, unpatched flaw in LMCache, a popular key-value cache layer used with vLLM. It's rated nine point eight out of ten.

In multiprocess mode, the cache server accepts messages over ZeroMQ and unpickles them before checking anything. Pickle is Python's serialization format, and loading untrusted pickle data can run arbitrary code. So anyone who can reach that port can run commands, and on the official images, the process runs as root.

Versions zero point three point nine through zero point five point five are affected, and there's no fix yet. The default binds to localhost, but LMCache's example Kubernetes DaemonSet listens on all interfaces.
So the action item: find any LMCache multiprocess servers, make sure they're only on localhost or a trusted cluster network, and don't rely on a firewall alone.
anthropic-usage-policy: Next, a governance change. Anthropic updated its usage policy yesterday.

There's a new section called Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes, which groups the rules against deceiving voters or disrupting elections. A separate rule bans broadly deceptive campaigns, like running fake accounts or fabricated news outlets. There are also new prohibitions around weapons software and surveillance.

The one getting headlines bans sustained and needless abuse of Claude. Anthropic says it only covers extreme, repeated cruelty with no purpose. It doesn't cover normal frustration, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.
For product teams, the practical step is to check any feature that generates political content or runs automated personas against the new language.
agent-epistemic-humility: Our last story is a study from Johns Hopkins about what they call epistemic humility in agents.

That just means: does the agent recognize when it's unsure, act on it, and tell you? They scored agents on three steps, identify the conflict, try to solve it, and escalate if it's still unresolved. They tested this with knowledge conflicts, where retrieved evidence contradicts what the model believes, or two sources disagree.

The finding is uncomfortable. Agents often noticed the conflict early, then lost track of it and handed back a confident wrong answer. And higher accuracy did not mean more humility. Fixes at the model level helped, but usually cost some accuracy.

The takeaway for teams is to add evals that check whether your agent flags uncertainty, not only whether it got the answer right. The authors say this depends on the model, the harness and the environment together.
outro: That's the brief. The big picture today: agents are getting identities, budgets and audit trails, and the security work around them is getting more serious.
If you run LMCache, check those ports today. Sources for every story are on the podcast page.
And I'm Leo. See you tomorrow.
